title: The Mark
subtitle: After Always · Chapter 22 of 40
content:
I saw the Dark Mark because Snape dropped a bottle of ink.

The fountain pen had become his favorite object despite his refusal to admit it. He used it for legal notes, research records, letters, and once, with grim satisfaction, a particularly scathing correction to a Ministry form.

The ink bottle slipped when his left hand cramped.

I caught the bottle.

He caught the table.

His sleeve pulled back.

Black lines surfaced against pale skin.

Not vivid the way they had been under Voldemort. Faded. Gray-black. A skull. A serpent.

The room stopped.

Snape yanked the sleeve down.

Too late.

I had seen it.

“I didn't mean to—”

“Spare me.”

His voice was ice.

I set the bottle upright.

“I was going to say stare.”

“You did.”

“Yes.”

He turned away.

The old Snape would have cut me with something sharp enough to make curiosity feel like a crime.

This Snape had changed enough to leave instead.

He made it three steps.

Then stopped.

“Do you want to see it?” he asked.

I stared at his back.

“Do you want me to?”

“No.”

“Then no.”

He turned.

His expression was angry.

“At least be honest.”

“I am curious.”

“Of course.”

“But curiosity doesn't outrank your no.”

His face shifted.

We had said versions of that before.

Touch. Memories. Rooms. Questions.

Boundaries had become the strange architecture of whatever we were building.

Snape sat at the table.

Slowly, he rolled his sleeve above the elbow.

“You said no,” I reminded him.

“I have changed my mind.”

The Mark lay on the inside of his forearm.

Faded did not mean gentle.

The shape was ugly in a deliberate way, branding made magical. It looked less like ink than something that had once lived beneath the skin and died there.

I did not touch it.

Snape watched my face.

“What are you waiting for?”

“Nothing.”

“You wanted to see.”

“I see.”

His jaw tightened.

“You may ask.”

“Does it hurt?”

“Not now.”

“Did it?”

“Yes.”

“When he summoned you?”

“Yes.”

“How bad?”

“Enough.”

I nodded.

“Does it ever feel like it's burning in dreams?”

His eyes sharpened.

“You remember.”

“Of course I remember.”

He looked away.

That seemed to affect him more than the question.

I studied the Mark again.

“Do you hate it?”

“Yes.”

“Do you want it removed?”

A pause.

“I do not know.”

That surprised me.

“Why not?”

He ran one finger just below the skull, not touching the lines.

“I wanted it once.”

The honesty hurt to hear.

“I was proud when I received it.”

I stayed still.

“I thought it meant I had been chosen.”

His mouth twisted.

“By the time I understood what it actually meant, I had already used the belonging it represented to do harm.”

“So keeping it is punishment?”

His eyes flashed.

“No amateur psychology.”

“It's after noon.”

He almost smiled.

Then didn't.

“Perhaps,” he admitted.

I leaned my forearms on the table.

“Could it also just be a scar?”

His gaze sharpened.

“What does that mean?”

“Not proof that you deserve suffering. Not proof that you're secretly good. Not a holy relic of regret. Just evidence that something happened to your body because of choices you made and a man who owned people through fear.”

Snape's face went still.

“Voldemort did not own me.”

“No?”

Anger rose.

Good.

I let it.

“He summoned you through your skin. Punished people for delay. Demanded obedience. Killed people who failed him. That sounds like ownership no matter how voluntarily someone walked in at the beginning.”

Snape's eyes were black and furious.

“I was not a victim in the sense you imply.”

“I didn't say you were innocent.”

“You imply coercion.”

“Later, yes.”

“I could have fled.”

“To where?”

“Anywhere.”

“Would he have let you?”

Silence.

“Would he have let anyone you cared about live?”

His throat worked.

“That is irrelevant.”

“No. It isn't.”

I softened my voice.

“You can be responsible for joining and still recognize what the structure became. Both can be true.”

He closed his eyes.

Our phrase.

When he opened them again, the anger had drained into exhaustion.

“You make everything intolerably complicated.”

“I thought that was your specialty.”

His mouth twitched.

I looked at the Mark.

“May I touch your arm?”

He froze.

The question sat between us.

“Why?”

“Because I want to.”

“Not the Mark?”

“Your arm.”

His breathing changed.

Then he turned his forearm upward on the table.

“Yes.”

I reached slowly.

My fingers settled against the unmarked skin near his wrist.

Warm.

A pulse beneath my fingertips.

Alive.

I did not trace the skull.

I did not try to erase it with tenderness.

I simply rested my hand there.

Snape watched.

His face became strangely vulnerable.

“Why?” he asked again.

“Because I like touching you.”

Color moved across his face.

“And because I wanted you to decide whether I could.”

His gaze dropped to my hand.

After a moment, his fingers moved.

He turned his arm, sliding his hand into mine.

The Mark disappeared beneath his sleeve again.

His hand remained.

We sat in the dungeon holding hands like two people who had somehow forgotten that this was supposed to be difficult.

Then Snape said, “Your palm is ink-stained.”

I looked down.

The spilled bottle had left a black streak across my fingers.

“So is yours.”

He examined his thumb.

“Careless.”

“Shared failing.”

“Do not become sentimental.”

“Never.”

He squeezed my hand once.

Later, the stain washed off.

The Mark did not.

He let me look at the Mark for less than five seconds.

That was longer than I expected.

It was not dramatic anymore. No burning black summons. No sudden agony. Just damaged skin and old magic, faded enough to look almost gray in the dungeon light.

“I thought it would disappear,” I admitted.

“So did several newspaper columnists. Their expertise in magical scarring was remarkable.”

“Does it hurt?”

“Occasionally.”

“When?”

His eyes flicked toward me.

“Relevant medical question,” I said.

“Cold. Exhaustion. Certain defensive spells. And when I have the misfortune to read the Daily Prophet.”

“That last one may be psychosomatic.”

“I assure you the pain is real.”

I smiled, then sobered.

“Do you hate it?”

“Yes.”

The answer was immediate.

“Do you hate your arm?”

That made him pause.

“No.”

“Good.”

His gaze sharpened. “Why?”

“Because it's still your arm.”

Something vulnerable crossed his face before suspicion covered it.

I did not touch the Mark. I touched two fingers to the inside of his wrist, well below it, after waiting for his nod.

His pulse beat against my fingertips.

“Still yours,” I said.

“Anatomically undeniable.”

I rolled my eyes.

He left his arm where it was.

I stopped wishing it would.
